claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are kinetically controlled.
Introducing a dwell at precursor-decomposition temperatures modestly increases atomic mobility.
The increased atomic mobility from the dwell enables homogeneous nucleation and locks in a metastable single-phase solid solution before segregation occurs.
Under standard rapid-heating and rapid-cooling conditions, a precursor mixture containing more than five noble metals undergoes phase separation and elemental clustering.
The intervention adds a controlled dwell at the precursor-decomposition temperature while otherwise preserving the rapid heating and cooling envelope.
Dwell times from near zero to several seconds should be explored at fixed composition and under an inert atmosphere.
Mobility during the dwell allows atoms to attain a uniform random distribution without reaching full thermodynamic equilibrium.
Full thermodynamic equilibration would cause phase separation in the targeted compositions.
Rapid heating and cooling leave insufficient atomic diffusion, which causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
A short dwell supplies enough diffusion for atomic mixing while retaining sufficient kinetic inhibition to favor a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Excessive dwell time permits near-equilibrium segregation.
An optimized dwell will produce a more uniform single-phase crystalline structure than the no-dwell baseline.
The dwell-treated nanoparticles may adopt a coherent FCC or related metastable phase.
An optimized dwell will reduce elemental clustering and improve morphological uniformity relative to the no-dwell baseline.
Longer-than-optimal dwell times will cause the onset of phase separation.
The applicable processing window is bounded by the precursor-decomposition temperature range and the maximum dwell time before equilibrium phase transformations dominate.
The intervention applies only to compositions sufficiently within the high-entropy regime to support metastable single-phase formation.
The optimal dwell time and temperature window depend on the precursors and elemental interactions.
Failure of an optimized dwell to improve phase uniformity, or failure of prolonged dwell to initiate phase separation, would falsify the proposed kinetic mechanism.
